title: Gosaikunda Yatra Guide for Pilgrims and Janai Purnima
meta_description: Gosaikunda yatra guide for pilgrims: Janai Purnima dates, walking route from Dhunche, helicopter yatra, holy dip, altitude safety, packing and costs.
summary: Gosaikunda (4,380 m) is a sacred lake of Lord Shiva, reached by a 2–3 day walk from Dhunche or a 35-minute helicopter flight from Kathmandu. The biggest yatra is on Janai Purnima, the August full moon. Walking pilgrimages cost from about ₹36,000 and helicopter seats from about ₹58,000 per person.

sections.heading: Why pilgrims go to Gosaikunda
paras: Gosaikunda is one of the holiest lakes in the Himalaya for Hindus. Tradition holds that after the churning of the ocean, Lord Shiva drank the deadly halahala poison to protect the world, and when it burned his throat he struck the mountainside with his trishul, releasing cold water that formed the lake. The Trishuli River is linked to that strike, and a rock in the lake is pointed out as Shiva resting. Many believe the lake's water flows underground to the Kumbheshwar temple pond in Patan.

Pilgrims come to bathe, offer puja at the small Shiva shrine on the shore, perform rites for ancestors and collect holy water. Tamang, Hyolmo and Tibetan Buddhists also consider the lakes sacred, and jhankri shamans from hill communities gather here at the August full moon. For Indian devotees, Gosaikunda pairs naturally with darshan at Pashupatinath and other Kathmandu temples.

sections.heading: When is Janai Purnima at Gosaikunda
paras: Janai Purnima falls on the full moon of the month of Shrawan, usually in August and occasionally in late July. On this day Brahmin and Chhetri men change the janai, the sacred thread, and people of all communities receive a raksha doro on the wrist from a priest. It coincides with Raksha Bandhan in India. At Gosaikunda, pilgrims arrive the day before, and the holy dip continues from the full-moon night through the next morning.

Because the date follows the lunar calendar, it shifts every year. Plan to leave Kathmandu three to four days before the full moon if walking, so you can acclimatise on the way up. If you prefer quiet, the same pilgrimage can be done from April to June or September to November, when the weather is clearer and the trail far less crowded. Check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Walking yatra or helicopter yatra
paras: There are two ways to reach the lake. Walking takes two to three days up from Dhunche through Chandanbari (Sing Gompa) and Lauribina, and one to two days down. It allows an overnight at the lake, a full holy dip at dawn and the festival atmosphere. The helicopter yatra flies from Kathmandu in about 35 minutes, lands near the shore for 20–40 minutes and returns. It suits older pilgrims and those short of time, but the stop is brief and weather can cancel flights.

sections.heading: The walking route day by day
paras: The standard pilgrim route begins with a 6–7 hour drive of about 117 km from Kathmandu to Dhunche (1,960 m), the district headquarters of Rasuwa. The first walking day climbs about 1,370 m through farmland and oak, rhododendron and fir forest via Deurali to Chandanbari (3,330 m), taking 5–6 hours. The second day climbs to Lauribina (3,910 m), and the third continues past Saraswati Kunda and Bhairab Kunda to Gosaikunda at 4,380 m.

Our recommended itinerary sleeps at Chandanbari and Lauribina before the lake, which keeps daily height gain safe, then spends the festival night at Gosaikunda. After the dawn dip, pilgrims descend to Chandanbari the same day and Dhunche the next, before driving back to Kathmandu. In total this is 7 days.
list: Day 1: Kathmandu to Dhunche by road, 6–7 hours
Day 2: Dhunche to Chandanbari, 5–6 hours walking
Day 4: Lauribina to Gosaikunda, 2–3 hours; festival night
Day 5: Holy dip and puja, descend to Chandanbari
Day 7: Dhunche to Kathmandu by road

sections.heading: Altitude and health for pilgrims
paras: Gosaikunda is at 4,380 m, higher than many pilgrims realise. Headache, breathlessness, poor sleep and loss of appetite are common, and serious altitude sickness can develop if you climb too fast. Walk slowly, drink 3–4 litres a day, avoid alcohol, and tell your leader at once about severe headache, vomiting, confusion or breathlessness at rest. The cure for altitude sickness is descent. Consult your doctor before travel about acetazolamide.

The water is near freezing even in August. Keep the dip to a few seconds, enter near the shore, and dry off and dress warmly immediately. Pilgrims with heart disease, high blood pressure, diabetes or breathing problems should take medical advice before booking and may be advised to sprinkle water rather than bathe, or to choose the helicopter.

sections.heading: What to pack for the yatra
paras: In August expect rain every day, leeches in the forest below Chandanbari, and near-freezing nights at the lake. Waterproof clothing and warm layers matter more than anything else. Pack light, as porters share loads, and keep puja items and holy water bottles in a dry bag.
list: Rain jacket, poncho and waterproof trekking shoes with good grip
Leech socks or salt, and long trousers tucked into socks
Down jacket, fleece, warm hat and gloves
Sleeping bag rated to −5 °C or lower
Towel and a full change of dry clothes for after the dip
Puja items, small bottles for holy water and a torch
Personal medicines, oral rehydration salts and sunscreen

sections.heading: Crowds, lodging and permits
paras: Thousands of pilgrims reach Gosaikunda over the festival days. Lodges at Chandanbari, Lauribina and the lake fill well in advance, food runs short and many people sleep in halls or tents. Our festival departures carry tents, mats and a kitchen crew so that the group has guaranteed shelter and hot vegetarian meals. Roads from Kathmandu are busy with pilgrim buses, and monsoon landslides can cause delays, so build in a spare day.

Gosaikunda lies inside Langtang National Park. Indian and other SAARC nationals pay a reduced entry fee of about NPR 1,500, against NPR 3,000 for other foreigners. Foreign trekkers need a licensed guide under rules in force since 2023; how this applies to Indian pilgrims has varied. Check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Adding Kathmandu temples to the yatra
paras: Most pilgrims combine Gosaikunda with darshan in Kathmandu. Pashupatinath, the great Shiva temple on the Bagmati, is the natural pairing, and many devotees offer the holy water they carry down from the lake here. On Janai Purnima itself, the Kumbheshwar temple in Patan holds a festival around its pond, believed to be fed by Gosaikunda through an underground channel, and Budhanilkantha, the sleeping Vishnu at the foot of Shivapuri, is another popular stop. Allow one or two days in Kathmandu before or after the yatra, which also gives a buffer for road delays or cancelled helicopter flights.

faqs.q: What is the best time for the Gosaikunda yatra?
faqs.a: For the festival, Janai Purnima in August. For clear weather and quiet trails, April to June or September to November. December to February is cold and snowy, with the lake frozen and the trail above Chandanbari often snowbound. Each season suits a different kind of pilgrim, so choose by priority.

faqs.q: How many days does the Gosaikunda yatra take?
faqs.a: On foot, plan 5–7 days return from Kathmandu, including the drive to Dhunche and acclimatisation nights. Our recommended pilgrimage takes 7 days. By helicopter, the yatra takes about 3 hours from Kathmandu, with a short stop at the lake for darshan and puja.

faqs.q: Is Gosaikunda yatra suitable for elderly people?
faqs.a: The walking yatra is demanding, with steep climbs to 4,380 m, so it suits only fit older pilgrims with medical clearance and a slow itinerary. The helicopter yatra is easier but still involves sudden altitude. Seniors with heart or lung problems should consult a doctor first and may be advised not to go.

faqs.q: How much does the Gosaikunda yatra cost?
faqs.a: A group walking pilgrimage of 7 days starts at about ₹36,000 per person, including transport, guide, porters, lodges or tents, meals and park fees. A shared helicopter seat starts at about ₹58,000, and a private five-seat charter costs roughly US$ 2,800–3,500. Festival-week prices are higher.

faqs.q: Can we stay overnight at Gosaikunda?
faqs.a: Yes. A few basic lodges on the shore offer dormitory and small rooms, and tents are used at festival time. Nights are near or below freezing, so a warm sleeping bag is essential. Staying overnight allows a dawn holy dip and the full-moon festival experience.

faqs.q: What is the significance of Janai Purnima at Gosaikunda?
faqs.a: On the Shrawan full moon, Hindus renew the sacred janai thread and receive raksha doro for protection, and bathing in Gosaikunda that day is believed to bring special merit and cleanse sins. Jhankri shamans perform through the night, and thousands of Hindu and Buddhist pilgrims gather.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide for the Gosaikunda pilgrimage?
faqs.a: Foreign trekkers need a licensed guide inside Langtang National Park under rules in force since 2023, and how this applies to Indian pilgrims has varied. In any case, a guide is strongly recommended because of altitude, monsoon conditions and festival crowds. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I combine Gosaikunda with Pashupatinath and Muktinath?
faqs.a: Yes. Many Indian pilgrims combine Gosaikunda with Pashupatinath and other Kathmandu temples, and some add Muktinath by flight or helicopter from Pokhara on a longer Nepal pilgrimage. Allow buffer days between them, as both Gosaikunda and Muktinath depend on weather.

faqs.q: Are there leeches on the Gosaikunda trail in August?
faqs.a: Yes, the forest between Dhunche and Chandanbari has many leeches in the monsoon. They are harmless but unpleasant. Wear long trousers tucked into socks, use leech socks or salt, and check your legs at each stop. Above Chandanbari, as the forest thins, leeches become rare.
